message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Must be returned within 30 days after you move out (unless you and the landlord agree otherwise).
• Landlord may keep money only for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear‑and‑tear, or other costs specified in the lease. | • Landlord must give a written itemized list of deductions.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit or provide an itemized statement, you can sue for the full amount plus damages. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity). | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the property in “good repair” and to fix any major problems that affect health or safety. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing if it’s longer than one year.
• The lease can’t contain illegal clauses (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable home). | • If the lease is silent on certain matters, Texas law fills in the gaps (e.g., the landlord must provide a working smoke detector). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if they’re stated in the lease and are reasonable. | • Texas law prohibits “unreasonable” late fees; courts have struck down fees that exceed 5% of the monthly rent. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must give written notice before filing an eviction suit.
• Common notices: 3‑day notice to pay rent or vacate, 30‑day notice to terminate a month‑to‑month tenancy, or 60‑day notice for longer leases. | • Eviction can only proceed after the court issues a writ of possession.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours’ notice before entering the unit (except in emergencies). | • Exceptions: emergencies, repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • This is enforced under the federal Fair Housing Act and Texas’ own Fair Housing laws. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (only if the lease allows it). | • The landlord must be notified in writing before you do this. | | **Retaliation** | • Landlord cannot retaliate against you for exercising your legal rights (e.g., reporting a violation). | • Retaliatory actions include raising rent, threatening eviction, or refusing to renew a lease. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • The lease may restrict subletting, but you can still negotiate with the landlord. | • If the lease is silent, you generally have the right to sublet unless the landlord has a valid reason to deny it. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • If the lease is silent, Texas law typically holds the landlord responsible for essential services (water, sewer, gas, electricity) unless otherwise agreed. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to carry insurance for your personal property. | • You may want renter’s insurance to protect your belongings. | --- #### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** - Look for clauses about rent, deposits, maintenance, entry, and termination. - Verify that any “special” provisions (e.g., pet fees, late fees) comply with Texas law. 2. **Document Everything** - Keep copies of all communications with your landlord (emails, texts, letters). - Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues or damage when you move in and out. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** - For example, a 3‑day notice to pay rent or vacate is required before a landlord can file an eviction action. - A 30‑day notice is needed to end a month‑to‑month tenancy. 4. **Use the Texas Attorney General’s Office** - They offer a free “Tenant’s Guide” and can help you file complaints against landlords who violate the law. 5. **Seek Legal Aid** - If you’re facing eviction or a dispute, local legal aid organizations can provide free or low‑cost representation. --- #### Quick Reference Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on fair housing, landlord‑tenant laws, and how to file complaints. | | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Guides for tenants, complaint forms, and enforcement actions. | | **Legal Aid of North Texas** | Free legal assistance for qualifying tenants. | | **Texas State Bar Association – Lawyer Referral Service** | Find a qualified attorney for a brief consultation. | | **National Apartment Association (NAA) – Texas Chapter** | Educational materials and advocacy for tenants. | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely return of your security deposit, clear lease terms, privacy, and protection against discrimination and retaliation. If a landlord violates these rights, you can seek remedies through the courts or state agencies. Always keep records, read your lease thoroughly, and know the notice periods required for any action. If you encounter a problem, use the resources above to get help and protect your interests.
